What if the real gap in digital energy innovation is not technology, but whether national innovation systems are enabling young builders in low-access settings?
 
That was at the heart of discussions today during the SDG 7 segment of the 2026 ECOSOC Youth Forum at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, alongside A. Anastasia Kefalidou and Elsy T. Milan.
 
Young people are already driving solutions in energy access, mini-grid management, and digital service delivery. But to unlock many of these ideas require to create national innovation systems that connect policy, financing and technology innovation to scale.
 
This matters because over 85% of the world’s youth live in developing countries where energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and unemployment are most acute, and where innovation needs stronger support.
 
Three reflections stand out:

	1.	Scaling digital energy systems requires solutions that reflect local realities. Southeast Asia’s AI startups attracted over USD 2 billion, but in places like the Pacific, where around 1,500 languages are spoken, tools that ignore local context may scale technically while failing in practice.

	2.	Youth innovation delivers most when energy systems are built to absorb it. Young innovators are already responding to local needs. In Kenya, Nigeria, and Rwanda, youth-led pay-as-you-go solar platforms are already using IoT and mobile money data to manage connections and improve planning.

	3.	Digital energy tools matter only if they advance real development outcomes. More than 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, while the world enters a multi-trillion-dollar digital infrastructure investment cycle. The real question is whether capital, data, and innovation are reaching the places where they can have the greatest human impact.

Young people are not waiting to be included in the transition. They are already building it. The task now is to align systems around them so their solutions can deliver at scale.
